VLANs help design networks with security in mind. A good network design balances security, performance, and reliability without sacrificing any single component.

&nbsp;

To use VLANs for security, we use security zones. A security zone groups network devices and controls how traffic moves in and out of that group.

&nbsp;

Network designers may use different names and rules for security zones. Here, we focus on the standard, commonly used security zones.

&nbsp;

The table below lists standard security zones to help you learn the basic terms:

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

| Security Zone | Description | Representative Examples |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **External** | Devices and connections outside the company’s internal network or control. | Web server clients |
| **DMZ (Demilitarized Zone)** | Separates untrusted public traffic and external connections from core internal systems. | Public-facing servers, BYOD devices, guest/remote access |
| **Trusted** | Houses internal computers and devices that do not handle sensitive data. | Standard workstations, B2B connections |
| **Restricted** | Protects critical systems, sensitive databases, and core infrastructure. | Domain controllers, confidential customer data |
| **Management** | Used for network administration and system control (often combined with the audit zone). | Virtualization platforms, backup systems |
| **Audit** | Used for security logging, monitoring, and tracking network activity (often part of management). | SIEM tools, telemetry systems |

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

In addition to internal traffic, you must control how new devices enter and interact with the network. Public web or email traffic stays in the DMZ, but remote users need safe access to internal systems. Access rules based on IP or MAC addresses can be set up and enforced using network security controls.

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

Security zones and access controls will physically direct how and where traffic goes. But how is it decided what resources users or devices have access to? Traffic rules are often governed by company security policy or compliance as equally as security controls that determine access permissions.&nbsp;

&nbsp;

&nbsp;

We’ve now established a system to approach designing VLANs, but how can we practically implement and enforce them? In the next task, we will cover several protocols and applications that can be used to implement and enforce VLANs.
